artboards.title: P1 — A line above the stack (leading)
P2 — Head of the M column

annotations.text:
Two lines per lane: name and M/S on the first, the fader under them.

That is EXACTLY the phone's lane, so there is now one lane shape at both widths and the breakpoint only decides whether the waveform is there — one DOM, one set of rules, half the CSS.

The gutter went 468px -> 312px -> 162px across the three passes, and the waveform took all of it: wide enough now to carry ticks every 30 seconds and 56px tall instead of 44px.

The colour chip beside each name is gone: the fader directly under it is already that instrument's colour, so the chip was saying it twice.

On the phone the halves go back to a full 44px each. Width is what the desktop gutter could not spare; height is what a thumb actually needs, and the phone has the room.

Per-lane waveforms still drop out here — one shared strip carries the position.

Play, clock and the preset share one line here too. At 390px that is about 345px of content in 350px — it fits, so the row WRAPS rather than overflows: a longer instrument set or a larger system font pushes the preset to its own line instead of off the screen.

Dropping the master removes a hazard as well as a row: playing it alongside the stems sums two copies of the same performance, which comb-filters at any timing error at all. It was only ever there to A/B against the reference, and the take page already plays it on its own.

One code follow-up: getMixData still appends it as a muted last track.
Kept for the record, not for building. B put long vertical faders first and gave up the waveform belonging to a track; C made the waveforms the interface and gave up balancing to a hover.

The time grid.

One list of ticks drives both the ruler labels and the lines, so a number and its line cannot disagree — and the labels sit at their true fraction of the take rather than being spaced evenly by the browser, which is how they drifted off the lines before.

Minutes take the #3A2413 hairline the rest of the app rules with; half-minutes take half that. Behind the waveforms, so a played portion covers the line and an unplayed one shows it through.

The clock sits in the ruler row now, in the cell above the track names — it reads the axis beside it, so that is the line it belongs on. The spread-in-milliseconds reading is gone: it was engine diagnostics, not something to read while playing.

The problem: play and “mute my instruments” float above everything, on no edge that anything else shares. They read as page furniture rather than as the mixer's controls — orphaned.

All three put the transport and the time measure on the same object. They differ in WHICH object.

T1 — ONE GRID. The transport sits on the lanes' own two columns: play and clock in the gutter, the ruler in the waveform column. Every row on the page then shares one vertical edge, and the clock is already beside the axis it reads.

“Mute my instruments” moves up beside the way out — it is a setting for the session, not a transport control, and it is what was making the row too wide to align.

Gives up: nothing structural. It is the quietest of the three, which is either the point or too quiet.

T2 — CONSOLE BAR. One bounded strip holds play, clock, ruler and the preset: a tinted fill and a hairline make it read as a piece of equipment sitting above the tracks.

Gives up: its internal rhythm is its own, so the ruler inside it does not line up with the lanes below — the grid that makes a timeline readable stops at the box. And it is the heaviest thing on a page whose system has no shadows and few boxes.

T3 — RULER CARRIES IT. No separate transport row at all: play sits in the gutter, and the CLOCK RIDES THE PLAYHEAD as a gold pill, so the number is always at the place it describes.

The preset shrinks to “Jen ostatní” (just the others) to fit beside play.

Gives up: a moving number is harder to read than a fixed one, and it collides with the tick labels it passes. The shortened preset label is also less clear than the sentence it replaces.

Where “mute my instruments” goes now that play and the clock own the gutter.

All three fix something T1 did not: nothing on this page says WHICH lanes are yours, so the preset's effect is unpredictable until you press it. Each direction answers that as well as placing the button.

P1 — A LINE ABOVE THE STACK. One quiet row between the ruler and the lanes: it names your instrument and offers the action on it.

It earns its height by saying something no other element does — “Bass je tvůj nástroj” — so the button's effect is known before it is pressed, and the label can be short because the sentence carries the meaning.

With several instruments it becomes “Bass a Organ jsou tvoje nástroje”, and with none the row simply is not there.

Gives up: a whole row, on a page that is already a stack of rows.

P2 — HEAD OF THE M COLUMN. The preset is a bulk mute, so it sits at the top of the mute column, in the same segmented shape as the M it operates. A person glyph marks your lanes.

The adjacency does the explaining: a ZTLUMIT sitting over a column of M buttons needs no sentence.

Gives up: it is small, and a column header on a table with no other column headers is a lone label. At 10px the word is also near the floor for a control.

P3 — BESIDE PLAY. A 34px icon button in the gutter, next to the transport it belongs with. Shown engaged here, so the Bass lane is muted and dimmed.

Cheapest in space by far, and it keeps every control on one line.

Gives up: the label. A person-with-a-cross glyph is a guess until you hover it, and this is the feature's whole reason for existing — the one control that should not need explaining is the one losing its words.
